chunks: And Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Faddal, from Ibn Bukayr, from a man from our companions, from a man who said:

I said to Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him): I said to my wife, 'You are upon me like the back of my mother,' if you go out from the chamber door. She went out. He said: 'There is no penalty upon you.' I said: 'I am capable of expiation.' He said: 'There is no penalty upon you.' I said: 'I am capable of expiating a slave or two slaves.' He said: 'There is no penalty upon you, whether you are capable or not.'

key_terms.إِخْرَاجُ الْمَرْأَةِ: The wife going out (the condition that triggers the Zihar in this context)
key_terms.الظَّهَار: Zihar, a form of divorce where a husband says to his wife 'You are upon me like the back of my mother'
key_terms.رَقَبَة: A slave (one of the forms of expiation in Islamic law)
key_terms.كَظَهْرِ أُمِّي: Like the back of my mother (the specific formula for Zihar)
key_terms.كَفَّارَة: Expiation (penance required for certain acts, such as Zihar or breaking an oath)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on expiation for Zihar if the wife leaves the house after the husband says the formula?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Al-Istibsar*, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies that the validity of *Zihar* does not automatically trigger the obligation of expiation (*kaffarah*), which remains a voluntary act for the husband unless he explicitly vows to perform it. This highlights the Shia juristic distinction between the establishment of the marital prohibition and the subsequent ritual penalty, emphasizing personal agency in religious obligations. The dialogue illustrates the precise conditions under which the husband's resolve ('I am strong/willing') determines the necessity of the expiation.
